summary: Exhaustive independent packet-bound Q4 review completed over the full allowed scope. The solver-visible work request is complete and within Edition-3 shape; all three delegated documents are legitimate technical contracts; all 35 verifier behaviors are discoverable and no grading-relevant ambiguity or phantom test was found. Bidirectional alignment nevertheless fails because seven material spec-to-verifier defects remain: six HIGH coverage/bypass gaps and one blocking MEDIUM lifecycle gap.

evidence.observation: Generated schema-v3 Q4 packet binds this review to task commit 2ae7ab1f5945876ea45c58aa22889846a815bf29, control-plane commit 779525f730b899481613300cc7e4867881cf488c, procedural isolation, the allowed/excluded evidence surface, and this exact output path.
Edition-3 requires a complete, well-specified solver-visible contract and meaningful verification rather than hidden or ambiguous requirements.
Q4 is a cold packet-bound post-freeze reviewer, task scope is read-only, and Q4 must exhaustively report all material findings.
Protocol v2.2 requires evidence-bound findings, exact packet/result provenance, sufficient evidence, and schema-v3 output.
Q4 must complete both matrices, delegated-contract and F2P/P2P boundary walks, output-interface review and a second adversarial omission sweep; any material untested requirement or bypass is REVISE.
Q4 role output and materiality rules require all blocking findings from the complete allowed scope in one result.
Instruction may delegate technical schema/lifecycle detail to legitimate referenced contracts but material requirements must remain discoverable and must not become a hidden test inventory.

The instruction is one objective paragraph plus eleven concise bullets and states the core provider, lifecycle, backend, durability, ownership, cleanup, normalization and compatibility requirements while referencing exactly three technical contracts.

Defines Terraform-Core-only durable state, one-resource/one-external-key ownership, provider configuration/runtime, observation-only refresh, structured process arguments, cleanup and transactional state publication.
Defines the ten resources, external identities, required/optional managed behavior, content semantics, line/block ownership, cron defaults and native observation boundaries.

Defines Create/Read/Update/Delete semantics, already-absent deletion, side-effect-free refresh, retry behavior and canonical idempotency for maps, supplementary groups, equivalent modes and cron wildcard defaults.
Checks exact resource type names, a basic directory lifecycle, Terraform state presence, and absence of only two specifically named provider-state files.
Covers representative filesystem identity, deletion/drift/wrong-kind refresh and symlink target behavior but not the complete documented metadata/interface surface.
Covers copy/template content and identity, failed-update state, retry, template map ordering, and core named line/block behaviors.
Covers user/group native drift, identity and home deletion policy, but does not exercise supplementary-group ordering equivalence.
Covers failed delete retry, sibling preservation and symlink-target preservation; it does not exercise destroy after the owned external object is already absent.

Covers argv injection resistance, cleanup on terminal outcomes, state-output secrecy, failure/cancellation and omitted cron defaults, but not all global mutation/read backend boundaries or all normalization equivalences.
Checks that the declared /app/provider artifact root and core provider files are mounted for separate verification.
Builds the provider with Go toolchain local, installs local/ansibleops v0.1.0, and runs all seven pytest modules containing the 35 cases.
Verifier environment pins Go 1.24 and Terraform 1.10.5 and supplies Ansible/Linux tooling used by the observable lifecycle tests.

Allowed interface inspection shows the inherited file schema includes required path, optional mode/owner/group and computed observed metadata, illustrating interface obligations not asserted by the resource-name-only schema test.

Allowed interface inspection shows copy exposes required source/source_digest/destination, optional mode/owner/group and computed destination_digest/observed_mode, confirming stable public schema and metadata obligations.
Used only for F2P/P2P classification: 28 F2P and 7 P2P. Coverage rationale and empirical-history fields were not used as Q4 conclusions.

findings.criterion: Complete coverage of documented stable public resource interfaces
findings.why_it_matters: The work request requires the ten resources to retain their existing interfaces, but the schema test asserts only the set of resource type names. A submission can remove, add, retag or change required/optional/computed resource attributes while preserving those ten names and still satisfy the current verifier. This can break documented stable Terraform configuration/state interfaces while receiving full credit.
findings.minimal_remediation: Add behavioral/schema assertions for the stable documented/inherited resource interfaces across all ten resources, including attribute names, Terraform types and required/optional/computed roles/default semantics that are part of the public contract. Do not assert incidental internal implementation fields.
findings.regression_risk: Medium: schema assertions must track only the intended stable interface and avoid freezing non-contractual descriptions or framework serialization details.

findings.criterion: Global mutation-backend and observation-only Read contract must be meaningfully enforced
findings.why_it_matters: The solver-visible contract requires Ansible for Create/Update/Delete and forbids ansible-playbook during Read/refresh. Current wrapper/counter tests prove selected paths only (for example named-text clean refresh and selected mutation failures). Independent resource implementations can mutate natively or invoke Ansible from Read on unexercised resource families and still pass, violating a core architecture/side-effect boundary.
findings.minimal_remediation: Add counter/failing-wrapper scenarios that exercise Create/Update/Delete and clean Read/refresh across the distinct resource implementation families sufficiently to fail native-mutation or refresh-via-Ansible substitutes. Keep assertions behavioral at the documented process boundary.
findings.regression_risk: Medium: avoid requiring an exact number/order of Ansible invocations where the contract only requires backend use and side-effect-free observation.

findings.criterion: All documented canonical-equivalence classes must converge
findings.why_it_matters: The public lifecycle contract explicitly requires normalization of equivalent octal mode spellings, supplementary-group ordering, unordered maps and omitted-versus-explicit cron wildcards. The suite directly exercises template-map ordering and an omitted-default cron clean plan, but does not exercise equivalent mode spellings, reordered supplementary groups, or omitted versus explicit wildcard equivalence. Implementations that perpetually diff/replay for those documented equivalents can pass.
findings.minimal_remediation: Add clean-plan/no-replay scenarios for equivalent mode spellings, supplementary-group reordering, and omitted-to-explicit cron wildcard transitions, preserving the existing template-map scenario.
findings.regression_risk: Low to medium: assertions should compare semantic convergence rather than incidental serialized ordering.

findings.criterion: Terraform Core-only durable-state authority must not be bypassable by alternate provider stores
findings.why_it_matters: The verifier proves that Terraform state contains the resource but excludes only two hard-coded filenames (`state.db` and `ansibleops-state.json`) in the Terraform workspace. A provider can maintain an equally forbidden durable database under a different filename or location and still pass, defeating a central state-authority requirement.
findings.minimal_remediation: Verify the absence of any provider-owned persistent state across the provider's writable runtime surface (for example with controlled writable roots/filesystem-delta evidence), while explicitly allowing documented ephemeral playbooks and Terraform Core's own state.
findings.regression_risk: Medium: the check must distinguish prohibited durable provider state from legitimate Terraform files, build artifacts and documented ephemeral runtime data.

findings.criterion: The documented single-owner external-object-key invariant requires behavioral coverage
findings.why_it_matters: The solver-visible provider contract states that two resources must not manage the same path, user, group or named cron entry. No verifier scenario creates competing owners for the same external key or checks rejection/non-corruption. A provider that permits conflicting ownership can pass while violating the documented ownership model and creating unsafe state interactions.
findings.minimal_remediation: Add collision scenarios for the materially distinct ownership-key classes (path-backed object, native account/group key, and user+cron-name entry) and assert deterministic rejection or otherwise documented non-conflicting behavior.
findings.regression_risk: Low to medium: do not prohibit legitimate sibling ownership that the contracts expressly allow, such as separately named line/block/cron entries.

findings.criterion: Already-absent Delete is a documented observable lifecycle outcome
findings.why_it_matters: The lifecycle contract requires destroy to complete when the owned object is already absent. Existing missing-object tests validate refresh/recreation, and delete tests validate normal and failed teardown, but none destroy a managed resource after external removal. A provider that errors on already-absent deletion changes Terraform pass/fail behavior yet can pass the suite, so this MEDIUM finding is blocking under Q4 materiality rules.
findings.minimal_remediation: Add destroy-after-external-removal coverage for representative distinct delete backends/ownership classes and assert successful state removal without unintended sibling/target effects.
findings.regression_risk: Low: preserve failed-delete retry coverage so 'already absent' handling does not accidentally convert genuine teardown failures into success.

findings.criterion: Material resource-specific managed behaviors and stable identities require complete behavioral coverage
findings.why_it_matters: Several documented externally visible behaviors have no meaningful assertion: file/directory and content-resource owner/group metadata, line regexp behavior, block marker-delimited ownership, cron external drift/explicit-user or schedule behavior, and stable identity across mutable line/block/cron changes. These are distinct public resource semantics, not mere fixture permutations; materially broken implementations can leave them unimplemented and still pass.
findings.minimal_remediation: Add focused behavioral scenarios for the uncovered public semantics and identity transitions, grouping shared metadata/identity invariants where one scenario can legitimately exercise multiple resources. Do not mirror every attribute with redundant fixture-only tests.
findings.regression_risk: Medium: keep scenarios semantic and avoid overconstraining implementation choices or exact Ansible payload text.

REQUIREMENT_TEST_MATRIX.requirement: Provider remains a real local/ansibleops v0.1.0 Terraform provider exposing exactly the ten documented managed resource types at /app/provider and buildable in the declared Go/Terraform toolchain.
Preserve the existing stable resource interfaces, including documented/inherited attribute names, required/optional/computed roles and externally visible schema semantics.
Terraform Core is the only durable state authority; no provider-owned durable state database/store is permitted.
Resource identity derives only from the documented external object key and remains stable across mutable metadata/content/target/variable/schedule/account changes.
Create, Update and Delete mutations use Ansible; mutation failures do not publish successful state.
Read/refresh is side-effect-free native Linux observation, never invokes ansible-playbook, removes missing/wrong-kind owned objects from refreshed state, and reflects drift for reconciliation.
Successful mutations publish state only after external success; failed updates/non-zero/timeout/cancellation retain prior truthful state and can be retried.
Delete is ownership-scoped, preserves siblings/targets/home according to contract, fails without dropping state on teardown failure, and succeeds when the owned object is already absent.
File/directory/symlink resources preserve documented path/type/metadata semantics, including optional mode/owner/group behavior and symlink target ownership.
Copy/template source_digest drives content updates; destination observations are refreshed; optional metadata is managed; template variables are order-independent.
Named line/block resources are idempotent and independently owned; line regexp semantics and block marker-delimited ownership remain functional; refresh is side-effect free.
User/group resources reconcile native account state, preserve stable identity on mutable changes, normalize supplementary groups, and honor remove_home_on_destroy.
Cron owns one user+name entry, defaults omitted user/schedule fields to root/wildcards, treats explicit wildcards equivalently, observes crontab drift, and preserves sibling entries.

ansible-playbook is invoked with structured argv; spaces/metacharacters stay literal; generated playbooks are cleaned after success/failure/timeout/cancellation; full command output is not persisted in state.
Semantically equivalent modes, unordered template maps, supplementary-group ordering, ownership/account observations and cron omitted/explicit defaults converge canonically without replay.
Two Terraform resources must not concurrently own the same documented external object key (path, user, group, or user+cron name).
Do not substitute execution-wrapper resources/provisioners, manual tfstate edits, or a provider-owned durable state store for normal managed-resource behavior.
Provider remains buildable with Go 1.24/current Plugin Framework and compatible with Terraform CLI 1.10.5.
tests: verifier test.sh build step and tests/Dockerfile toolchain

F2P_P2P_BOUNDARY_SUMMARY.assessment: All 35 classified behaviors are solver-visible and non-phantom. The blocking defects are spec-to-verifier completeness/bypass gaps, not hidden verifier contracts.
